Reference adversary (claude): reference_wrong. For 2026, R.C. 5747.02 sets Ohio's tax at $332 plus 2.75% of taxable income above $26,050. That base accounts for the consensus's whole $332 shortfall, so the consensus ($1,589.56) is wrong. The engine has the base, the two $1,900 exemptions and the $200 retirement income credit right. However, it starts from Ohio AGI equal to federal AGI ($94,925.30) and takes no medical-care deduction under R.C. 5747.01(A)(10)(b). On the stated facts the head paid $6,500 of non-employer insurance premiums and $800 of other medical costs, totaling $7,300. Premiums count as medical care under IRC 213(d)(1)(D), and $7,300 exceeds 7.5% of federal AGI ($7,119.38), so the deduction is about $180.63. Ohio tax after the retirement credit is then about $1,916.60, roughly $5 below the reference. Engine step at issue: Determining Ohio AGI of $94,925.30. The engine applied no R.C. 5747.01(A)(10)(b) deduction for unreimbursed medical care above 7.5% of federal AGI, even though the head's $6,500 of after-tax non-employer premiums plus $800 of other medical expenses exceed that threshold.

The 133–211% band, the former NC Health Choice population, came into Medicaid in 2023 as Medicaid-expansion CHIP under the optional targeted low-income child group (42 CFR 435.229), and that group's definition in 42 CFR 435.4 excludes any child covered under a group health plan. Child 1 has employer-sponsored insurance.

Reference adversary (claude): reference_wrong. For tax year 2026, Colorado law (C.R.S. 39-22-2003) allows the state sales tax refund only if there were excess state revenues for the fiscal year ending in that tax year, which is FY 2025-26. Every official projection before the freeze, including the June 2026 Legislative Council Staff forecast, had FY 2025-26 revenue $424.9M below the Referendum C cap, with no refund obligation, so that refund is $0. The head is 66 and childless, so no federal EITC means no CO EITC, and there is no CO CTC, FATC, senior housing credit or other refundable credit. The engine's $19 is all sales tax refund. It is the published tax year 2025 lowest-tier single-filer amount carried into 2026, an amount 2026 law does not support. The law gives $0, which matches the consensus. Engine step at issue: The engine allowed the Colorado sales tax refund ($19, computed from MAGI of $4,625.40) for tax year 2026. It applied the tax year 2025 refund table without the statutory condition that FY 2025-26 revenue exceed the TABOR/Referendum C cap. That condition was not met: it was projected unmet before the freeze and certified unmet in September 2026.

Reference adversary (claude): reference_wrong. Under the law in force for 2026, this household gets about $1,188 in refundable NY credits. The first part is the Empire State Child Credit of $307: $1,000 for a child aged three or younger, less 42 × $16.50 for federal AGI above $75,000. The second part is the new refundable NY child and dependent care credit of about $881 under Tax Law § 606(c-2), added by L.2026 ch.59 Part A and signed 2026-05-28: $3,000 of expenses × (55% − 0.00025 points per dollar of NY AGI above $15,000) ≈ 29.35%. The engine's ESCC is correct. For child care, though, it applied the old § 606(c) credit (60% of the federal credit, $360), which by its own terms now covers only tax years beginning before 2026. So the $667 reference rests on a repealed rule. Engine step at issue: New York's child and dependent care credit is $360: 60% of the federal credit (20% of $3,000). This is the pre-2026 § 606(c)(1) computation, which L.2026 ch.59 limited to tax years beginning before 2026-01-01 and replaced with the § 606(c-2) credit on qualifying expenses.

Reference adversary (claude): definition_mismatch. Pennsylvania taxes each dollar of income at a flat 3.07%, with no deductions or exemptions. The parents' joint PA-40 covers $100,002 of income, for $3,070.06 of tax. The 16-year-old has $45,000 of wages and must file a separate PA-40, owing $1,381.50. Tax forgiveness is $0 at these incomes, so the household owes $4,451.56 in total. The engine's $3,070.06 is correct for the parents' return, but it treats the child only as a dependent and never computes the child's own required return. The output definition does not limit itself to one return, and the prompt says to assume filing where required, so the engine leaves out a return the definition covers. The output should be excluded, or recomputed to include the child's return. Engine step at issue: The engine starts from the tax unit's IRS gross income of $100,002 (head and spouse only) to get pa_total_taxable_income. It drops the dependent child's $45,000 of wages and models no separate PA-40 for the child, so the child's $1,381.50 of PA tax is missing from state_income_tax_before_refundable_credits.
